title: LoveShackFancy Talks Target Collaboration, Growth Strategy and the Art of Successful Partnerships
text:
Rebecca Hessel Cohen and Stacy Lilien discuss what makes a partnership thrive, expanding into new categories, and building brand love across generations.
, and Stacy Lilien, president of the company, talked about what constitutes a good collaboration and what they’re looking to accomplish when the lifestyle brand teams with a partner.more than 200 items across apparel, accessories, beauty and school supplies“One of the things we love most about strategic partnerships is the opportunity to bring LoveShackFancy to new audiences,” Lilien said.
“We keep a close eye on what’s resonating with the tween and teen customer and how she’s discovering and engaging with brands today. This collaboration with Target gave us the opportunity to take everything people love about LoveShackFancy and translate it into a back-to-school collection that feels fun, accessible and collectible. ” Most items are priced under $25.
LoveShackFancy, founded in 2013 by Hessel Cohen, offers fashion, beauty, childrenswear, accessories, home and lifestyle products that are known for their romantic, vintage-inspired aesthetic and devoted following. In addition to 30 directly owned boutiques in the U.S. and London, the brand is found in 450 retailers worldwide. In a Q&A with Hessel Cohen and Lilien, they spoke about what makes a collaboration successful and what they are looking for when they enter a partnership.
: If it introduces LoveShackFancy to someone new and it still feels unmistakably us, that’s a win. Sales matter, obviously but a successful collaboration should drive real customer acquisition and open us up to new growth categories. The real marker is whether she falls in love with the brand because of the collaboration and stays a customer long after it ends. : We generally look for partners in a category we’re interested in testing, to determine demand.
Beyond that, we’re constantly listening to our community, what’s trending and what she’s asking for. Kendra Scott, for example, made sense because our customers were already cross-shopping us on RushTok . Stanley made sense because it had become this viral object for a generation of girls, and we wanted to be part of that conversation. Roller Rabbit made sense because we wanted to test the market for pajamas and lounge.
At the end of the day, it has to bring something fresh and unexpected to our girl, and give us a real signal on whether the category is worth pursuing further.. : Stanley! Stanley is still one of the top search terms on our site. Our first launch, two years ago, was one of the largest sales days in our brand’s history as well as Stanleys, which is remarkable considering Stanley itself has been around since 1913.
There’s something powerful about pairing a hundred-year-old heritage object with something that feels totally of-the-moment.. : Last year we did 20 collaborations. This year, we’re anticipating a similar number, but we’re being more strategic about timing and launch cadence, making sure each one has room to breathe rather than competing with the next.. : It’s distribution without diluting the dream.
Every collaboration is a door into LoveShackFancy for someone who might not otherwise walk into one of our boutiques, visit our site or follow us on social; each one functions as a customer acquisition channel with a built-in audience already in place. She meets us first through a Stanley cup, or a Kendra Scott necklace, or bedding at Pottery Barn and, eventually, she finds her way to the dresses.. : It really depends on the brand and the specific collaboration.
In general, we try to be a true partner and stay hands-on through every step of the process. Our brand is defined by a distinct visual language — pink, florals, bows, femininity — and a collaboration typically brings those elements to the forefront. The partner brings their category expertise and their audience; we bring the romance and the world of LoveShackFancy.. : I actually don’t see it that way.
We realize that we are a prestige brand and our main line isn’t accessible to everyone due to the fabrics we use, the factories we produce in and the quantities we make. We hear constantly from girls who are dying to get their hands on LoveShackFancy, and a partnership like this lets us meet them there. I wanted to bring the feeling of LoveShackFancy to more girls, not fewer.
It also gave us the chance to partner with purpose beyond the collection. Yoobi’s Buy One, Give One model means every qualifying item purchased puts a product directly into the hands of a child in need, distributed through their partnership with Kids in Need Foundation. To date, the LoveShackFancy x Yoobi collaboration has donated 2.1 million units and 5,000 classroom packs, reaching over 152,000 kids across the country..
: These collaborations give us the opportunity to see how our girl responds to something new, a real-time test of the market before we commit. It’s usually categories we don’t make ourselves.
For example, Roller Rabbit and Pink let us test intimates and lounge, which saw incredible growth. Home came through Pottery Barn.. : The majority of our collaborations are super limited edition; they come in as capsules or drops. In general, scarcity is part of what makes them work.
But we also have an incredible long-term partnership with Pottery Barn, sold exclusively through their channel.. : Bogner, without question. The epitome of skiwear and decades of European heritage. I started skiing with my family the same year we launched our first Bogner collaboration, and having florals on the slopes made me love skiing and après.
Seeing all that print out on the mountain, in a sea of black and navy…it was so refreshing and fun.. : Dylan’s Candy Bar. Dylan grew up in New York. I’ve been obsessed with Ralph Lauren since I was a kid, and she loves to celebrate just as much as I do.
Therefore, a candy collaboration for Valentine’s Day felt like the most us, least expected pairing we could do. It sold out fast, which told us our girl wants LoveShackFancy in categories we’d never even think to put ourselves in.. : We don’t disclose specific deal terms, but collaborations make up roughly 10 percent of our overall business, meaningful, but not the core of what we do. WWD: What age group are these aimed at?
When have you gone outside your target customer, and how did it go?. : Our main line skews a wide demo. We often say “babies to 80s,” and that’s not a slogan, it’s who our customer actually is. But the limited-edition collaborations are a chance to be extremely culturally relevant and tap into the zeitgeist, which often skews us younger, since that’s where the cultural conversation is happening and where things go viral.
Together, they let us stretch in both directions without ever losing the center of who we are. WWD and Women's Wear Daily are part of Penske Media Corporation. © 2026 Fairchild Publishing, LLC. All Rights Reserved.
